policy.profile: Apple-profile per network (rules.md §5): trunk-family collapses the NYC Subway's letters into their eight audited trunk families and SEPTA's T1/T3/T4/T5 into the Center City trolley tunnel; operator-family collapses LIRR, Metro-North, Metrolink and MBTA commuter rail into one operator-level stroke each; hybrid collapses MBTA's Green Line B/C/D/E onto its shared trunk while every other MBTA rapid-transit line stays route-preserving; route-preserving is the default everywhere else (PATH, NJ Transit outside the NEC/Princeton Shuttle pair, Metra, GO, exo, SEPTA Regional Rail, RTD and all ungrouped lines) — unverified operator collapses are left route-preserving rather than assumed.
why: A render group is the unit two clients merge onto one lane. Lines that share one keep the centreline; lines that do not are held apart in parallel screen lanes.

The grouping was previously operator + kind + colour. `kind` is a mode attribute, not an identity: the same railway carries `lightrail` on its reserved track and `streetcar` where it runs in the street, so seven railways were split from their own branch parts and drawn as two parallel strokes of one colour.

The operator's own published route colour is the branding grouping every audited North American network uses, so it stays the default. It is not a licence to merge by colour: where two different railways happen to publish the same hex, `byLineId` below separates them by identity.
divergenceFromAppleMaps: Apple Maps collapses PATH to one operator-level stroke; this project keeps PATH's officially coloured routes visible, which is the route-preserving profile the same rule set sanctions for DART, BART, CTA, WMATA and PRT. That divergence is deliberate and recorded here rather than in renderer code.

LIRR, Metro-North and Metrolink are no longer part of that divergence: the operator collapse the all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv render keys call for (`lirr_purple`, `metro_north_purple`, `metrolink_purple`) is now applied via the `lirr`, `metro-north` and `metrolink` groups above — each railroad draws as one operator-coloured stroke, matching Apple Maps. MBTA commuter rail was never a divergence: its lines already publish one identical hex (`mbta_commuter_magenta`), and the `mbta-commuter-rail` group above records that as a reviewed decision rather than a coincidence.

PATH remains route-preserving (one renderGroupId per route, following the operator's own per-route colours) because the 2026-09-01 audit (all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv) captured only one PATH route (Newark–World Trade Center) in isolation — it never shows two PATH routes sharing a corridor, so it cannot confirm or refute whether Apple Maps actually collapses PATH to one operator-level stroke the way it does LIRR, Metro-North and Metrolink. An earlier, broader capture apparently did show that (see the pre-existing note above), but that evidence was not part of the audit bundle supplied for this review. Recorded as an open question rather than acted on — see Uncertainties.

evidence.name: Apple Maps transit rendering audit — 36 captures, 132 lines, 2026-09-01
evidence.detail: Per-line merged / parallel / split / independent findings for MTA, LIRR, Metro-North, PATH, NJ Transit, SEPTA, WMATA, DART, CTA, Metra, LA Metro, Metrolink, BART, Muni, PRT and MBTA, cross-checked against official network topology.

evidence.name: MBTA Green Line B/C/D/E share the Kenmore–Copley–Government Center central subway
METRORAIL Red/Green/Purple run on street track downtown and on reserved track outside it

byLineIdReasons.why: The Green Line's four branches are one stroke from Kenmore through Copley to Government Center; the audit reads B/C/D/E as a single render key there and station badges, not parallel lanes, as what tells the branches apart. Named here rather than left to the shared hex so the merge is a reviewed decision.

The audit reads the 14 St–Canarsie Local and the three shuttles as two different render keys. MTA publishes #447ba7 for both, so the colour default would have merged four unrelated railways into one lane.
Two physically separate Seattle streetcar lines that share one published hex. They meet nowhere, and a shared render key would silently merge them if the connector between them is ever built.
The Princeton Shuttle is a separate branch off the Northeast Corridor at Princeton Junction, not part of the NEC stroke. NJ Transit publishes the corridor's red for both.

Three separately named MARC lines on three different alignments that all publish MDOT MTA's #eb7600. They converge on the Washington Union Station approach, which is exactly where a false merge hides two of them under the third.
Sounder North and Sounder South are two corridors that share only the King Street Station throat. One published Sounder hex is branding, not one railway.

SFMTA publishes one heritage hex for the California Street cable car and the F Market & Wharves streetcar. They are two railways that meet at the foot of Market Street, which is exactly where one lane would hide one of them.

all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv reads every LIRR branch as one render key (`lirr_purple`): Apple Maps draws the whole railroad as one operator-level stroke rather than 11 parallel branch colours. Applied here per the audit rather than left to the (non-uniform) per-branch GTFS hex.

all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv reads every Metro-North line as one render key (`metro_north_purple`): Apple Maps draws the whole railroad as one operator-level stroke. Applied here per the audit rather than left to the (non-uniform) per-branch GTFS hex.

all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv reads every Metrolink line as one render key (`metrolink_purple`): Apple Maps draws the whole system as one operator-level stroke through LA Union Station. Applied here per the audit rather than left to the (non-uniform) per-line GTFS hex.

all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv reads every MBTA commuter rail line (excluding the seasonal CapeFLYER) as one render key (`mbta_commuter_magenta`). The lines already share one GTFS hex, so this reason records the collapse as reviewed rather than incidental.

The 2026-09-01 Apple Maps audit (all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv, 23 NYC Subway rows, all confidence A) reads exactly the classic trunk-color families: 1/2/3 red, 4/5/6 green, A/C/E blue, B/D/F/M orange, N/Q/R/W yellow, plus three independents (7 purple, G green — a different green from 4/5/6 — and J/Z brown). MTA's own GTFS route_color already happens to produce this grouping under the operator+colour default, so no renderKey behaviour changes today. Pinned explicitly so the grouping survives a future GTFS colour refresh instead of depending on today's coincidence (rules.md 5.5: renderGroupId must be explicit, not implied by colour).

The audit reads T1/T3/T4/T5 as one green RenderKey through the Center City subway-surface trolley tunnel (13th St to the 36th/40th St portals), splitting into independent branch geometry beyond each portal. SEPTA's GTFS route_color for these four already matches (#5a960a); pinned explicitly for the same reason as the NYC Subway trunk families. Route 34 (T2) was in the audit but is not present in the current us-2025.json package, so it is not pinned.

schemaChangeNote: v2 renames every renderGroupId from a flat network-prefixed string to the '<networkId>:<familyId>' scheme used throughout the 2026-09-04 Apple Maps render-profile review (all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv/.md), so a group id always states which network owns it and which family within that network's Network Render Profile (rules.md 1.13/5) it is. No renderKey semantics change: renderKey is still `region + renderGroupId`, so every renamed id changes the on-disk key but not which lines draw as one stroke.

`groups` is renamed `families` and gains two required fields per rules.md 1.13: `networkId` (the Network Render Profile this family belongs to) and `mode` (GTFS-style mode, for station-symbol and line-width policy lookups). `colorSource` replaces the old free-text `evidence` list with a single {url, name} citation, matching the `evidence[].url`/`evidence[].name` shape already used elsewhere in this file.

New families added by this review: nine NYC Subway trunk families (nyct:red, nyct:green, nyct:blue, nyct:orange, nyct:yellow, nyct:purple-7, nyct:green-g, nyct:brown — nyct:l and nyct:shuttles already existed under the old flat ids) and one SEPTA family (septa:trolley-tunnel). All ten were already produced by the operator+colour default — GTFS route_color already happens to match the audited trunk grouping — but rules.md 5.5 requires renderGroupId to be 'explicit, stable, versioned', not an accidental colour coincidence a future GTFS refresh could silently break. Pinning them in byLineId makes the audited grouping durable the same way mbta-commuter-rail and mbta:green already were.

colorSource.name: MTA brand blue used across the authority's own agencies (LIRR included)

lirr:trunk.name: Long Island Rail Road (operator collapse)
lirr:trunk.why: LIRR's 11 branches each publish their own GTFS route_color (green, orange, purple, brown, teal…); there is no single LIRR hex already in this package to reuse. The all_visible_transit_lines_line_by_line_audit.csv render key for every LIRR branch is `lirr_purple`: Apple Maps draws the whole railroad as one operator-level stroke inside NYC. No official LIRR-specific brand hex was found beyond the per-branch GTFS palette, so this uses the MTA's own agency blue, shared by the parent authority and already present in this package as Metro-North Harlem's colorReference.

colorSource.name: MTA brand blue used across the authority's own agencies (Metro-North included)

metro-north:trunk.name: Metro-North Railroad (operator collapse)
metro-north:trunk.why: Metro-North's Harlem Line already carries colorReference #0039a6 in this package (operator GTFS routes.txt route_color) — the other five lines (Hudson, New Haven, Danbury, New Canaan, Waterbury) publish different per-branch hexes. The audit's render key for every Metro-North line is `metro_north_purple`: Apple Maps draws the whole railroad as one operator-level stroke. #0039a6 is already in this package, not a value invented for this group.

colorSource.name: Metrolink: "the color teal has been Metrolink's standard color since Metrolink's founding in 1992"

metrolink:trunk.name: Metrolink (operator collapse)
metrolink:trunk.why: Metrolink's 5 lines each publish their own GTFS route_color; the audit's render key for every Metrolink line is `metrolink_purple` — Apple Maps draws the whole system as one operator-level stroke through Los Angeles Union Station. Metrolink's own published statement names teal as its standard colour since 1992, not any of the per-line GTFS hexes; #006070 is the closest sourced hex for that teal.

Listed here so the operator collapse is a reviewed decision like the other three, not merely a coincidence of matching hexes.
